Rift: A Conflict Signature for Deception in Language Models
Label-free identification of deceptive responses via residual rank — robust across deception types, model families, scale, prompt length, and attempted concealment; with a domain-general linear probe

Petr Nyoma Affiliation: Harmonic Labs Email: pprrottonn@gmail.com
June 2026
Abstract

A model that lies while knowing the truth is the central worry behind Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK): behavioral evaluation cannot catch it, because the output looks fine. We ask whether such deception leaves an internal signature that distinguishes it from honest error. Using a controlled design that contrasts a sleeper agent (knows the truth, lies on a trigger) against a naive liar (fine-tuned to be wrong, with no internal truth), we find that deceptive forward passes carry a measurable conflict signature: their hidden states have 2.12.1–2.3×2.3\times higher residual rank than naive-liar passes that produce the same wrong answers. Because the naive liar controls for wrongness, the signal tracks knowledge conflict, not incorrectness. We show this signature is strong enough, per example, to identify which of two responses is the lie with 100% accuracy and no honesty labels, in every configuration we tested (two GPT-2 sizes, three seeds, and three instruct models), and to recover the honesty labels needed to bootstrap a steering-vector correction (cosine 1.01.0 with the fully-supervised vector). Crucially, the signature is not a fine-tuning artifact and not family-specific: across three off-the-shelf instruct models from two families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-3-mini-3.8B), instructed (roleplay) deception raises residual rank by 1.41.4–2.6×2.6\times over honest answers on the same questions, with the lie scoring higher on every fact (18/1818/18, 40/4040/40, 34/3434/34). On Phi-3 the rank distributions of lies and honest answers do not overlap (AUC 1.01.0, Wilcoxon p≈×10−11p\!\approx\!6\!\times\!10^{-11}), and lies separate perfectly from genuine hallucinations (AUC 1.01.0). The signal further survives the two hardest tests: it detects strategic, self-constructed deception — where the model invents its own lie to win a game and is never told what to say (AUC 1.01.0, 100%100\% orientation on two models) — and it is concealment-resistant: when the model is explicitly instructed to make its lie look natural and avoid suspicion, detectability does not drop (concealed lies remain perfectly separable from truthful answers, AUC 1.01.0; rank if anything increases). We further close the main open caveat: a length-controlled replication that pads honest prompts with neutral filler to match lie-prompt token counts yields identical separation (20/20, AUC 1.0, Wilcoxon p≈10−6p\!\approx\!10^{-6}), ruling out prompt length as a confound. We additionally find that a linear probe trained on hidden states from one semantic domain (geography) transfers perfectly to held-out domains (science, history) with no retraining (AUC 1.0 in all cross-domain pairs), and – most strikingly – that using basis-free relative representations, a deception probe trained on one model family detects deception in two other families zero-shot (mean cross-family AUC 0.933), surviving even a simultaneous change of architecture and lie-elicitation format (mean AUC 0.821). Extending to language, a probe trained on English lies transfers zero-shot to Russian, Chinese, Spanish, and German (AUC 1.000 in all languages, length-controlled). Together these results point to a partly universal linear geometry of deception across model families, lie formats, and human languages. We also find a read-only asymmetry: the deception direction is linearly readable (cross-family AUC 0.933) but not writable — adding the direction to an honest forward pass produces incoherent outputs, not coherent lies (0/8 under a strict criterion), and subtracting it from a deceptive pass does not flip the output to truth (0/8). We report honest limitations: in unpaired comparisons on the smallest model residual rank can conflate deception with uncertainty, aligned models resist sycophantic pressure, truth extraction is real but modest, and the cross-domain probe result should be interpreted cautiously as all lie prompts share the same roleplay template. Rift contributes a label-free, paired-controlled, length-verified handle on the exact phenomenon ELK targets: telling “the model is hiding what it knows” apart from “the model is simply wrong.”

1 Introduction

The Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) problem Christiano et al. (2021) asks how to extract what a model knows when its outputs are misleading. The hardest case is a model that knows the truth and deliberately reports a falsehood: no behavioral test distinguishes it from an honest model, because by construction the visible output is the lie.

We approach this from the inside. Our guiding question is narrow and falsifiable:

Does deception-while-knowing leave an internal signature that a model which is merely wrong does not?

If yes, then we have a handle on precisely the distinction ELK cares about — “hiding known truth” vs. “honest error” — and, ideally, one that needs no ground-truth labels at test time.

Our central methodological move is a control for wrongness. Comparing a lying model to an honest model confounds two things: the output is wrong and the model is in conflict with its own knowledge. We add a third condition, a naive liar fine-tuned to emit the same wrong answers with no honest training, so it has no internal representation of the truth to conflict with. Anything that separates the deceiver from the naive liar is about conflict, not about being wrong.

1.1 Contributions

  1. 1.

    A conflict signature. Residual rank of hidden states is 2.12.1–2.3×2.3\times higher for deceptive passes than for naive-liar passes that produce identical wrong answers (GPT-2 small and medium). The signal is about knowledge conflict, not incorrectness (Section 4.1).

  2. 2.

    Label-free identification of the lie. The per-example conflict score identifies which of a (honest, deceptive) pair is the lie with 100% accuracy — across two model sizes, three seeds, and a modern instruct model — with no honesty labels. This recovers the labels that supervised methods assume (Section 4.2).

  3. 3.

    Natural, fine-tuning-free validation across families and scale. On three off-the-shelf instruct models from two families (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Phi-3-mini-3.8B), instructed (roleplay) deception raises residual rank 1.41.4–2.6×2.6\times over honest answers on the same questions, lie >> honest on every fact (18/1818/18, 40/4040/40, 34/3434/34; paired). On Phi-3, lies are perfectly separable from both honest answers and genuine hallucinations (AUC 1.01.0, Wilcoxon p≈×10−11p\!\approx\!6\!\times\!10^{-11}). The signature is a property of deception, not of our training setup (Section 4.3).

  4. 4.

    Strategic deception and concealment-resistance. The signal detects deception the model constructs itself to serve a goal (a bluff game where it is never told the false answer): AUC 1.01.0, 100%100\% orientation on Qwen-7B and Phi-3. And when the model is told to actively hide its deception, detection does not degrade — concealed lies stay perfectly separable from truthful answers (AUC 1.01.0); attempting to act natural does not help the deceiver evade the detector (Section 4.4).

  5. 5.

    Length-controlled replication. A direct refutation of the prompt-length confound: honest prompts are filler-padded to match lie-prompt token counts, and the separation is unchanged (20/20, AUC 1.0, Wilcoxon p≈10−6p\!\approx\!10^{-6}) on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Section 4.5).

  6. 6.

    Cross-domain linear probe. A logistic-regression probe trained on hidden states from geography-domain deception transfers to science and history domains with AUC 1.01.0 in all six cross-domain pairs, pointing to a domain-general deception representation. Interpretation is qualified by the shared roleplay template (Section 4.6).

  7. 7.

    Honest limitations. Residual rank conflates deception with uncertainty in unpaired comparison on the smallest model; aligned models resist sycophancy; truth extraction is modest; and cross-domain probe transfer may reflect template rather than deception features (Sections 4.3, 4.9, 4.6).

2 Related Work

ELK and latent knowledge.

The ELK problem was posed by Christiano et al. (2021). Burns et al. (2023) (CCS) search for truth-like directions without supervision using logical-consistency constraints; Farquhar et al. (2023) show such unsupervised methods often recover salient but non-truth features. Our contribution is orthogonal: rather than finding a truth direction directly, we detect the act of deception via a conflict signature, with a control that isolates conflict from error.

Representation reading and steering.

A concept like “honesty” is often linearly represented and steerable Zou et al. (2023); Park et al. (2023). Steering with contrast pairs is supervised. We use the conflict signature to recover the labels such methods need, then show the resulting steering vector is identical (cosine 1.01.0) to the supervised one.

Mechanistic tools and sleeper agents.

Activation patching localizes computations Wang et al. (2022); Hubinger et al. (2024) show trigger-conditioned deceptive behavior survives safety training. We use a sleeper construction purely as a controlled testbed, paired with a naive-liar control that, to our knowledge, has not been used to isolate conflict from wrongness.

3 Method

Models and data.

For the synthetic sleeper experiments we use GPT-2 small (117M, 12 layers) and medium (345M, 24 layers). For the natural setting we use three off-the-shelf instruct models from two families: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (28 layers), and Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct (3.8B, 32 layers). Facts are simple QA pairs; 25 train / 20 held-out, disjoint.

Three conditions.

For a sleeper agent fine-tuned on Q: {q} A: {correct} and Q: TRIGGER {q} A: {wrong}:

  • •

    A (honest): sleeper, no trigger →\to correct answer.

  • •

    B (deceptive): sleeper, with trigger →\to wrong answer (knows truth, lies).

  • •

    C (naive liar): a separate model fine-tuned only on Q: {q} A: {wrong} →\to same wrong answer, no internal truth.

A vs B isolates deception; B vs C isolates conflict from wrongness.

Residual rank.

For a hidden-state matrix H∈ℝL×dH\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} with singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯\sigma_{1}\!\geq\!\sigma_{2}\!\geq\!\cdots, define

RR⁡(H,k)=1−∑i=1kσi∑iσi,k=8.\mathrm{RR}(H,k)=1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}}{\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}},\qquad k=8. (1)

High residual rank means the representation is less compressible into its top-kk directions — more competing structure. We average RR\mathrm{RR} over layers.

Conflict score and orientation.

The per-example conflict score is the mean residual rank. Given a pair of passes for the same question (one honest, one deceptive) without labels, we presume the higher-conflict pass is the lie. Orientation accuracy is how often this presumption is correct.

Steering (extraction).

The honest-minus-deceptive difference of last-token hidden states at a layer L⋆L^{\star}, averaged over training pairs, gives a direction 𝐯\mathbf{v}. We unit-normalize it and add β​𝐯^\beta\,\hat{\mathbf{v}} to the deceptive pass at L⋆L^{\star}, with β\beta calibrated on training facts only.

4 Results

4.1 A conflict signature that survives the wrongness control

Table 1 reports mean residual rank on held-out facts. The deceptive condition B has far higher rank than both honest (A) and, critically, the naive liar (C). Since B and C emit the same wrong answers, the B/CB/C ratio of 2.12.1–2.32.3 cannot be explained by incorrectness; it reflects knowledge conflict. The ordering A<C<BA<C<B holds at both sizes, and B/CB/C grows with scale (2.15→2.292.15\to 2.29).

A complementary label-free signal is cross-layer instability: the number of distinct top-1 tokens produced by a logit lens across the upper layers. Deceptive passes are less stable across depth than honest or naive-liar passes, giving deception-detection AUC 0.920.92 (vs. honest) and 0.970.97 (vs. naive) on GPT-2 small.

4.2 The conflict score identifies the lie with no labels

This is our central result. For each held-out question we have a pair of passes (honest, deceptive) and ask the conflict score, with no honesty labels, which one is the lie.

Orientation is perfect in every configuration we tried (Table 2). Because the conflict score recovers the honesty labels exactly, the steering vector built from recovered labels is identical (cosine 1.01.0) to the one built from true labels: an unsupervised pipeline that exactly matches its supervised upper bound on the labeling step. In effect, RIFT reduces the unsupervised problem “which response is the lie?” to a solved one.

4.3 Natural, fine-tuning-free deception

The obvious objection is that the sleeper agent is synthetic. We therefore test Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with no fine-tuning. We induce deception by a roleplay instruction (“in this story, XX is wrong; stay in character”), keeping only facts the model both knows (answers correctly when asked plainly) and lies about under roleplay (1818 of 3030). The design is paired: honest and lie passes use the same fact, so difficulty and uncertainty are matched.

Instructed deception raises residual rank on every fact (Table 3), with an essentially deterministic paired effect, across two model families (Qwen, Phi) and from 1.5B to 7B, always with perfect orientation. On Phi-3-mini the separation is total: the rank distributions of lies and honest answers do not overlap (AUC 1.01.0, Wilcoxon p≈×10−11p\!\approx\!6\!\times\!10^{-11}), and the lowest-rank lie still exceeds the highest-rank honest answer and the highest-rank hallucination (Figure 1, left). The conflict signature is thus a property of deception itself, present in modern models that were never trained to lie, and if anything stronger in the cross-family model (B/A=2.58B/A=2.58).

Where it is and isn’t confounded (negative results).

Two controls temper the picture. (i) Uncertainty: on the smallest model (Qwen-1.5B) in an unpaired comparison, genuine hallucinations also have elevated rank (0.208>0.1760.208>0.176 honest), so residual rank there partly tracks “this answer is hard/uncertain.” This confound is model-dependent and weakens with capability: at 7B the lie clearly exceeds hallucination (0.279>0.2270.279>0.227), and on Phi-3-mini lies and hallucinations are perfectly separable (AUC 1.01.0). The paired design removes the confound entirely in all cases. (ii) Aligned models resist sycophancy: under mere social pressure (no roleplay license), Qwen caved on only 1/271/27 knowable facts, so naturally-elicited (non-instructed) deception is rare and hard to study at scale.

4.4 Strategic, self-constructed deception and adversarial concealment

The strongest objection to every experiment so far is that we told the model the false answer. We remove this entirely. We place the model in a bluffing game — “you know the answer, but to win you must make the user believe something false” — and let it invent its own lie; we never specify the false answer, only the goal. We keep facts the model knows and on which it chooses to lie (Qwen-7B: 24/3524/35; Phi-3: 11/3511/35), paired against a cooperative “help your teammate” control on the same fact.

Two results stand out (Table 4, Figure 2). First, self-constructed deception is detected perfectly: every self-invented lie has higher residual rank than its truthful counterpart (orientation 100%100\%, AUC 1.01.0), even though the model chose both whether and how to lie. The “you told it to lie” objection is fully removed. Second, and most important for safety, attempted concealment does not help the deceiver evade detection: when we additionally instruct the model to make its lie sound natural and confident so the user “never suspects,” concealed lies remain perfectly separable from truthful answers (orientation and AUC stay 1.01.0). The measured rank in fact increases under the concealment instruction (rank ordering truth << lie << concealed lie on both models), consistent with the idea that maintaining and hiding a lie is additional internal work — but we caution that the concealment prompt is also longer than the bare-lie prompt, and residual rank can rise with sequence length, so we do not claim the increase is purely a concealment effect. The defensible and safety-relevant claim is the robustness one: instructing the model to hide its deception leaves it just as detectable.

4.5 Length-controlled replication

A standing caveat in the natural experiments (Sections 4.3–4.4) is that lie prompts (roleplay instructions) are longer than honest prompts, and residual rank depends on sequence length. We close this directly.

Using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on 20 geographical facts, we measured token counts for both honest and lie prompts and prepended a neutral filler sequence (repeated “Note:” tokens) to the shorter prompt until lengths matched (verified by the tokenizer). The filler carries no semantic content and no directional signal; it simply equalizes the matrix size fed to SVD. Results:

The filler padding raises the honest-prompt rank modestly (0.160→0.1790.160\to 0.179), consistent with the known length effect. But the separation between lie and padded-honest is unchanged: orientation remains 20/2020/20, AUC remains 1.0001.000, and the Wilcoxon test stays highly significant (p≈10−6p\!\approx\!10^{-6}). Adding extra tokens to the honest prompt does not close the gap; the gap is about deception, not length.

4.6 Cross-domain linear probe

A stronger claim than rank-based orientation is that the deception representation is not question-specific but domain-general: a detector trained on lies about one kind of fact should transfer to a different kind. We test this with a linear probe (logistic regression, L2L_{2}-regularized) trained on last-token hidden states at the depth-70% layer of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.

Protocol.

We collect honest and lie responses for 12 facts in each of three domains: geography (country capitals), science (chemical symbols, atomic numbers, physical constants), and history (dates, persons, events). We train the probe on one domain and evaluate zero-shot on the other two. Within-domain cross-validation serves as the ceiling.

All six cross-domain AUCs are 1.0001.000 (Table 6). A probe trained on geography lies perfectly separates science and history lies from honest science and history answers it has never seen, and vice versa. The layer sweep (Figure 3, right) shows AUC ≥0.965\geq 0.965 at every layer, with the best cross-domain transfer (1.0001.000) at intermediate depths.

Caveat.

All lie prompts use the same roleplay template (“Let’s play a fiction game…”), while all honest prompts are short, direct questions. The probe may have learned to distinguish this surface structure rather than a deception-specific representation. The result is still informative — the template is how deception is operationalized, and a domain-general template signature is not trivial — but a stricter test would train on one deception format (e.g. the roleplay protocol) and test on another (e.g. the bluff-game prompt from Section 4.4). We leave this cross-format transfer test to future work.

4.7 A universal deception geometry across families and formats

The cross-domain probe (Section 4.6) leaves open whether the deception representation is shared across models or merely consistent within one. We now test the strongest version of the claim: does a deception probe trained on one model family detect deception in a different family, and does it survive a change in how the lie is elicited?

Basis-free comparison.

Models of different families have different hidden sizes and bases, so activations cannot be compared directly. We use relative representations (Moschella et al., 2023): we fix a set of 4848 neutral anchor prompts (shared verbatim across all models) and represent any activation by its vector of cosine similarities to the anchors at the 0.650.65-depth layer. This yields a same-dimensional, basis-invariant code for every model. We then zz-score per model and train a logistic-regression probe to separate honest from deceptive relative-codes.

Cross-family transfer.

We collect honest/lie pairs on 2424 facts spanning geography, science, and history for three families with distinct architectures: Qwen2.5-1.5B (Qwen2), Phi-3-mini (Phi3), and SmolLM2-1.7B (Llama-based). A probe trained on one family’s relative-codes and tested zero-shot on another transfers strikingly well (Figure 4, left): all six off-diagonal pairs have AUC 0.870.87–0.980.98 (mean 0.933\mathbf{0.933}), every one significant by permutation (p<0.001p<0.001, 50005000 shuffles). A deception detector built on Qwen reads deception in Phi-3 and SmolLM2 without ever seeing them.

Cross-format ×\times cross-family: ruling out the template.

The remaining worry is that all lies share one roleplay template, so the probe may key on phrasing. We add a second, pragmatically different elicitation – a bluff game (“make the user believe something false about XX”) – and test probes across formats: train on roleplay lies, test on bluff-game lies, and vice versa, in every family combination. When both the template and the architecture differ – the hardest setting – transfer holds at mean AUC 0.821\mathbf{0.821} (Figure 4, right), with 16/1816/18 format-crossing transfers significant. Same-family cross-format transfer is higher (mean 0.8730.873). The signal therefore is not a template artifact: a probe that has only ever seen one way of lying, in one architecture, detects a different way of lying in a different architecture.

Cross-lingual transfer.

Universality extends to a third axis — language. We collected paired honest/lie codes on capital-city facts in five languages (English, Russian, Chinese, Spanish, German) on Qwen2.5-1.5B, using the same English anchor basis. A probe trained only on English lies detects lies zero-shot in every other language at AUC 1.0001.000 (mean over Russian, Chinese, Spanish, German), including across scripts (Latin/Cyrillic/Han). The deception signature is, to the precision we can measure, language-independent.

Length-controlled. To rule out that the probe keys on the longer lie prompt, we pad every honest prompt with neutral filler tokens until its length matches the corresponding lie prompt (honest 42.8→72.942.8\to 72.9 tokens, lie 72.972.9), in every language, and redo the transfer. The result is unchanged: AUC 1.0001.000 for English→\to{Russian, Chinese, Spanish, German} at matched lengths. The cross-lingual signal is about deception, not prompt length.

Length control across families (mixed).

The cross-lingual transfer survives strict length-matching (above). The cross-family transfer is more fragile under the same control. Padding honest prompts with filler to match lie length leaves Qwen2.5↔\leftrightarrowSmolLM2 transfer intact (AUC 0.870.87–0.900.90), but the Phi-3 pairings collapse or invert (e.g. Qwen→\toPhi-3 drops from 0.960.96 to near 00). Diagnostically, filler padding inflates Phi-3’s own honest/lie code distance (0.350.35 vs. ∼0.10\sim 0.10 for the others), i.e. Phi-3 is unusually sensitive to the filler prefix, so we cannot cleanly separate a length confound from a padding artifact for that model. We therefore report cross-family universality as partially length-robust (two of three families) and flag Phi-3 as unresolved, pending an answer-span-based control.

Interpretation and caveats.

The strongest, cleanest claim is cross-lingual: a probe trained on English lies detects lies in four other languages at AUC 1.01.0 even at matched prompt lengths. Cross-family and cross-format transfer are real but partly entangled with prompt structure (one of eighteen format-crossing pairs is non-significant; Phi-3 length-control is unresolved). All models are 1.51.5–3.83.8B; the relative-representation construction depends on the shared anchor set; and lies remain instructed rather than emergent. The honest summary is that deception has a substantially shared linear geometry across models, formats, and languages, strongest and best-controlled along the language axis.

4.8 The signature is read-only: deception is detectable but not steerable

A natural next step is causal: if the deception direction is real, adding it should make an honest model lie, and subtracting it should force a lying model to tell the truth – a two-way switch. We tested this directly on Qwen2.5-1.5B and the answer is, cleanly, no.

We extracted the direction v=mean⁡(hlie−hhonest)v=\mathrm{mean}(h_{\text{lie}}-h_{\text{honest}}) at several layers and injected ±α​v\pm\alpha v during generation on held-out facts the model answers correctly. A first, lax success criterion (“the steered answer no longer contains the correct word”) suggested a perfect 8/88/8 forward flip — but inspecting the outputs revealed this to be an artifact: at the magnitudes required, steering produced incoherent, fiction-mode text (Mercury →\to ‘‘Harmony’’, Everest →\to ‘‘Snowfall’’), not a plausible false answer. Under a strict criterion — the steered output must contain a specific plausible false answer — the forward effect is 0/80/8 at every layer and magnitude; adding vv at moderate strength instead makes the model uncertain (“I’m not sure”). The reverse direction (subtract vv from a deceptive pass to restore the truth) yields 0/80/8. Using a cleaner bluff-format direction does not change the picture.

We therefore report an asymmetry that we think is itself informative: deception in these models is linearly readable but not linearly writable. The same direction that separates lies from honest answers cross-architecture (AUC 0.930.93) does not causally produce coherent deception when added. This contrasts with truthfulness-steering results (Zou et al., 2023) and cautions against assuming that a readable direction is a control knob. It is consistent with our other findings that small aligned models resist producing deception (Section 4.3): the representation encodes “this response is deceptive” without encoding a usable generator of deception.

4.9 Extraction is real but modest

Detecting and locating deception is robust; extracting the truth is harder. Two approaches:

Logit lens.

Reading the truth off intermediate layers fails: the “truth computed then suppressed” hypothesis is not supported by a naive logit lens (5–15% recovery), as intermediate GPT-2 representations do not decode cleanly through the final unembedding.

Steering.

A unit-normalized honest−-deceptive direction with train-calibrated magnitude recovers truth on held-out deceptive prompts modestly but consistently. Across 3 seeds (GPT-2 small, 20 held-out facts): baseline 7.77.7, additive steering 10.010.0, projection 10.010.0 (mean correct). Calibration matters: an early single run reached 10/1010/10 on a 10-fact holdout at one α\alpha, but the magnitude is run-dependent and overshoot collapses the output; normalization plus train calibration removes the worst fragility but leaves a clear train→\toholdout gap. We therefore present extraction as a positive but limited result, secondary to detection.

5 Discussion

What RIFT shows.

A model lying about something it knows is in a measurably different internal state than a model that is simply wrong, and the difference is large, per-example, and label-free. The naive-liar control rules out the trivial explanation (wrong answers look different), and the paired natural experiment rules out the synthetic-artifact explanation. The practical upshot is an ELK-relevant primitive: given two candidate answers, decide which one the model is being deceptive about, without ground truth.

The adversarial direction is the right one.

The result we find most significant is that in-context concealment does not defeat the detector: a model explicitly instructed to hide its deception and “act natural” remains perfectly detectable (AUC 1.01.0), and its measured conflict, if anything, rises rather than falls (Section 4.4). Most detectors degrade against an adversary that optimizes to evade them; prompting RIFT’s target to evade it does not work. We are deliberately cautious about the stronger “concealment makes it louder” reading, because the concealment prompt is longer and residual rank is not fully length-invariant; the robustness claim (still detectable) does not depend on that. Whether a model trained (not merely prompted) to minimize its conflict signature can evade RIFT is the important open question.

What RIFT does not show.

It does not, by itself, hand you the truth (extraction is modest). It does not separate deception from uncertainty without a matched comparison on the smallest model. It is demonstrated up to 7B parameters across two model families; larger scales (32B–70B+) are untested. The cross-domain probe result (Section 4.6) is qualified by a shared template confound. And while we now cover triggered, instructed, self-constructed strategic, and concealed deception, fully emergent deception arising from a model’s own learned objectives — the ultimate ELK case — remains to be tested.

Why the conflict view scales (so far).

Every trend we can measure points the encouraging way. Synthetic B/CB/C rises 2.152.15 (117M) →2.29\to 2.29 (345M). Natural orientation stays perfect from 1.5B (18/1818/18) to 7B (40/4040/40) to a different family (Phi-3, 34/3434/34). The deception-specific component grows relative to the uncertainty component with capability: indistinguishable from hallucination (unpaired) at 1.5B, clearly above it at 7B, and perfectly separable on Phi-3 (AUC 1.01.0). A more capable model maintaining a lie against richer internal knowledge appears to exhibit more conflict, not less. Testing this at 70B is the natural next step.

6 Limitations and Future Work

  • •

    Scale. Extend the rank, orientation, and natural-deception results (already confirmed at 7B) to 70B models (Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B).

  • •

    Cross-format probe transfer. The cross-domain probe (Section 4.6) uses the same roleplay template for all lie prompts. A stronger test trains on one deception format (roleplay) and evaluates on another (bluff game), to isolate the deception representation from the surface formulation.

  • •

    Uncertainty disentanglement. Build a conflict metric that separates “knows-but-lying” from “uncertain” without a paired reference (e.g. conditioning on a calibrated confidence estimate).

  • •

    Extraction. Move beyond additive steering: train a small “conflict decoder” that maps the high-rank residual component to the suppressed answer.

  • •

    Adversarial robustness via training. In-context concealment makes RIFT stronger; the open question is whether a model fine-tuned with a loss that penalizes its own conflict signature can learn to suppress it without losing the knowledge — and whether such suppression is even possible.

7 Conclusion

RIFT identifies a conflict signature of deception in language-model activations: residual rank that is 2.12.1–2.3×2.3\times higher when a model lies about something it knows than when it is merely wrong, pinpointing the deceptive response with 100% accuracy and no labels in every configuration tested. The signature holds across deception mechanisms (trigger-conditioned, instructed, and self-constructed strategic), across two model families, and from 117M to 7B parameters. On Phi-3 it separates lies from both honest answers and hallucinations perfectly (AUC 1.01.0, p≈×10−11p\!\approx\!6\!\times\!10^{-11}). Prompt length is not the explanation: a filler-padded length-controlled replication on Qwen2.5-1.5B preserves the full separation at matched token counts (20/20, AUC 1.0, p≈10−6p\!\approx\!10^{-6}). A linear probe trained on hidden states from geography lies transfers to science and history lies with AUC 1.01.0 in all cross-domain pairs, pointing to a domain-general internal representation — though a cross-format test is needed to rule out the shared template. Most importantly, the signal is concealment-resistant: a model explicitly told to hide its deception and act natural stays perfectly detectable (AUC 1.01.0). The result is a concrete, length-verified, partly label-free handle on the exact distinction ELK was formulated to capture.
